text: 929. (a) Tir. padə, padī ‘foot’, Wg. pad ‘foundation of a house’ (cf. Garh. pai ‘foundation’); note PAN pɔdmɔ̄ś ‘swelling of the foot’ with second syllable < OIA *macya- ‘growth (?)’ (9710) (with deaffrication) < OIA padá-¹ ‘footstep; site, abode, home’ (7747). (b) Kann. potalaṅg (pó-ta-lang) or pōtlöṅ ‘the sole of the foot’ < OIA pādatala- ‘sole of foot’ (8059). Here, however, the -t- may have survived due to a contraction of the -dat- sequence. (c) Bur. badá ‘sole of foot; step, pace’ borrowed from OIA padá-¹ ‘footstep’ (7747); here perhaps also Bur. padáaỵ -̇t- ‘to kick a stone with the foot’; note also Brah. pād ‘leg, foot (confined to compound words)’ and Bal. phāð. A repeatedly reborrowed OIA word. (d) Note also Munda padaʔ padaʔ ‘bounding, jumping along’ (Kuiper [1965: 81]).

text: 1067. Bng. phusi n.f. ‘female genitals’, Kṭg. and Kc. phʊ́ssi, phʊ́śṭi ‘female genitals’, Him. fusi, Paṭṭ. phəṣu ‘vagina’, Kann. phēċ ‘vagina’ — Bur. pháṣi ‘whore; woman, who is continuously coming and going’, Bur.ng. phóṣi ‘vagina’, Paš. phisū ‘vulva’ and perhaps Kal. kaphusi ‘witch’ (with a negative prefix) and Brah. pas ‘pudendum’. According to Turner (see Addenda and Corrigenda) < OIA *phussa- ‘defective’ (9100) and *phissa- ‘defective’ (9081), but this cannot be correct. There is also Gadd. pussī ‘darling’, but a possible connection with OIA *puśśī- ‘cat’ (8298) in a way comparable to English pussy ‘cat; female genitals’ (with parallels in other European languages) is not cor- roborated by Baṅgāṇī language consultants. According to Southworth (2005b: 13), this lemma may actually be a borrowing from Dravidian pucci ‘vulva’ as also found in M. pucci; however, there are also Southern Kiranti Bantawa phu ci ‘vulva, vagina’ and West Himalayish Kann. phɛ̄ċ ‘vulva’. An ex. from the Mid-West Himalayas: the beginning of a regionally well-known song which is sung in the night of the carnival-like ‘Old Diwali’ festival about a girl named Sungri: sungri ɛ phusɛ kɛ pã̄sru pelɛ kɛ gāṇḍi - cũ̄ cā Sungri hey pussy at ribbon penis at bell ring ring ‘hey Sungri, at your pussy is a ribbon at (the boy’s) penis is a bell - ding dong’

text: 1076. Bng. and Deog. bɔk-bɔk ‘bleating of a goat’ — Ind. bʌ̀x-bʌx karʌ́ṽ ‘to bleat as a male goat during rutting season’, Bhat. bækbæk gæry ‘to prattle useless things’, Bur. boq ét- ‘to bugle, call (ram in mating)’, Wg. babakā- ‘to make a mating call (male goats)’ — S. ɓoka ‘cry of a goat’, Mult. bāk ‘bleat of sheep or goat’, L. bok ‘bleat of a goat’, Jaṭ. ɓok ‘lust, lasciviousness’ (sub OIA *bokka- ‘he-goat’ [9312]), Brah. bōking ‘cry of the he-goat when covering’. Cf. Orm. baɣ and Yid.-Mj. baɣaz ‘bellowing, bleating’, and Sant. bhek bhek ‘to bleat as a goat when hurt’. Influenced by derivations of (or even derived from) OIA *bokka- ‘he-goat’ (9312). This word is itself possibly a Central Asian borrowing (Witzel [2005: 107]) or rather of Caucasian origin (cf. Common Kartvelian *buk’w- ‘billy goat;- one-year-old goat’ and cf. Tsova- Tushian [Bats] language bωok’ ‘billy goat/one-year-old goat’, but there is a strong onomatopoeic dimension.

text: 1295. Khāśi. metrër, metrelā ‘stepmother’ < OIA *mātr̥tarā- ‘stepmother’ (10022); regarding Srk. matərma ‘stepmother’, Jaṭ. matrˈimā ‘stepmother’ and Maṇḍ. māhtimī ‘woman’ cf. RV mātŕ̥tama- ‘very like a mother’. The Khāśi. form is remarkable for preservation of the syllabic -r̥-, and the lemma is remarkable for its closeness to Lat. matertera ‘maternal aunt’ and (slightly less close) Gr. μητρυιά ‘stepmother’ (see IGN: 80 and Martrirosyan [2013: 112]). Cf. also Brah. mātuna ‘stepmother’, Arm. mawrvi ‘of a stepmother’ (Mann [1963: 39]) or mauru ‘stepmother’ (IGN: 80) and Psht. maira ‘stepmother’ for which Morgenstierne, however, reconstructs Av. *māθryā-. Still, note also that there are several NIA languages with similar sounding words, however with meaning ‘mother’, e.g. Aw. mahᵃtārī.

text: 1343. Bashg. ruganâ ‘a fir-tree’, Kho. roɣ ‘light’, Brah. and Bal. rŏ̄k ‘light’, Dm. rāk, Kal. of Urtsun rak (also ᵃrak) ‘deodar’, Garh. rã̄ko ‘torch; bright light’, N. rã̄ko ‘torch’ < OIA róka- ‘light’ (10826). There is also Yid. rōɣo ‘deodar’. Note: Here cognate is also Khaś. reś ‘a kind of fir tree’ (Kaul [2006 i: 334]) < OIA rocya- ‘shining(?)’ (10835) with a parallel in Gaw.

text: 1373. S. las ‘sickle’ < OIA lavítra- ‘sickle’ (10988)? This would require a process similar to that found in West Pahāṛī: -tr- > -c- > sibilant which is indeed supported by Brah. laššī ‘sickle’ because Brah. has preserved two of the three OIA sibilants in its IA borrowings; cf. also Sh.gil. lēc̣ ‘reaping’. A possible parallel to this deaffrication is found in S. cīr and sīr both ‘a split’ < OIA cí̄ra- ‘strip’ (4843) and in S. surko ‘vinegar’ (also Ko. sirko and M. śirkā) < OIA cukrá- ‘vinegar’ (4850).

text: 1389. Bng. lepɔ2 n.m. ‘stick’, lepiaṭhɔ n.m. ‘a stone or piece of wood used outside to throw after cattle’, lupiaṭhɔ n.m. ‘baton, truncheon’ (with -iaṭhɔ suffix), lupiaṇɔ and lɔpṛiaṇɔ ‘to beat’ (with -ṛia- intensive suffix) are perhaps result of a contamination of OIA *lappa-² ‘slap’ and LUP ‘destroy’ (cf. also lepṇɔ ‘to peel etc.’ [p. 853]) because of closely related Bng. repṇɔ ‘to beat, push away’, repṛiaṇɔ ‘to chase away s.o.’ (with -ṛia- intensive suffix) and rɔpṛiaṇɔ ‘to push away (object or person)’ (with same suffix; is different from rɔpṇɔ ‘to seize’ see p. 845), and repiaṭhɔ n.m. ‘baton, truncheon, stick used to chase away s.o.’ (also with -iaṭhɔ suffix); here also Brah. rip ‘ricochet’ and perhaps also Ko. rip ‘lath’. This suggest derivation < the parallel root RUP ‘destroy’ which is semantically different from OIA RUP ‘pierce’ reflexes of which are given above p. 705.

text: 1494. Bng. śikɔ n.m. ‘top, peak; trophy’ — Brah. šik ‘pointed’ < OIA *sr̥kka- ‘arrow, spear’ (13575) perhaps with a modern parallel in Mth. This proposal presupposes a sound change sr̥ > ś which indeed has a parallel in Bng. śɔṛīk n.f. and Kṭg. śɔṛək both ‘road’ which are < OIA sr̥tí- ‘road’ (13577).  Notes: (a) This sound change is, for obvious reasons, little known from mainstream IA sound history – cf. sraṁs ‘fall’ v.l. śraṁs – but it parallels several cases of PIE *sr > ś respectively ṣ quoted in this book (cf. e.g. the lemma ‘to slurp’ [p. 855] and other examples p. 473) and it parallels processes largely limited to the northwest: OIA srávati ‘flows’ (13880) > K. śravun ‘to drip’, OIA srasta- ‘fallen’ (13882) > Kho. (Lorimer) šərʌst ‘quickly’ (?), OIA srāváyati ‘causes to move’ (13885) > Pr. -ṣu- ‘to suckle, suck’ and same root in OIA *prasrāvayati ‘causes to flow forth’ (8891) > Brah. (as loanword) pōšing ‘to suck’, OIA srutí- ‘road, path’ (13887) or srotiyá̄- ‘stream’ (13890) perhaps > Wg. ṣūī ‘ravine, valley’. The data suggests that this process, which is an alloform of RUKI, was limited to the northwest and west at a very early stage. In addition it suggests that the RUKI rule conflated in the northwest with a rule of coronal consonant harmony “dissimilation of st (and later, čt) to št in K. and Kal. [i.e. Wg.]; e.g., K. štˈum ‘tree . . . ” (see above Strand p. 476). (b) An alternative analysis of Bng. śikɔ < OIA śíkhā- ‘tuft, topknot, crest’ (12436) (Pa., Pk.) with -kɔ1 suffix seems also possible, and there is Ku. poet. śikh ‘tuft, topknot(?)’ (Meissner [1985: 217]). Related is also Bng. śikurɔ, śikrɔ, śikuri n.m.,n.f. ‘treetop’, either with k(h)rɔ suffix or cognate with OIA *śikkhara- ‘point, peak’ (12435), cf. also Pr. čirˈīg ‘tree top; Wipfel’; here an ex. from a Bng. song: ċīl śikuri-ɛ sɔ̄rɛlɔ mevarɛ pine-tree top-on sparkle.FUT.M.SG snow-covering ‘on top of the pine tree sparkles the snow covering’ Note that sɔ̄rṇɔ ‘to shine, sparkle’ could be cognate with OIA SVAR ‘shine’, the existence of which, however, Mayrhofer (EWA) doubts. The word mevarɛ ‘snow covering’ could be a compound, cf. OIA (BhP) mihikā- ‘snow’ (lex. also ‘mist, fog’) which is the same as OIA (TBr.) miháikā- probably ‘cloud’ (see EWA sub meghá-). Background of second component is unclear.

text: 1508. Here follow two different semantic fields (‘fly’ [as bird] and ‘hiss’ [as snake]) with com- mon origin in OIA ŚVAS ‘breathe’ (śuṣi-² *‘breath’): (a) Klm. šĩ̄š dǟg H ‘to fly’ and šĩ̄š-diant H-H ‘(he) is flying’ belong to Klm. šĩ̄š ‘breath’ and are therefore cognate with OIA ŚVAS ‘breathe’, more precisely with śuṣi-² *‘breath’ (12547) (with same vowel change as e.g. in Woṭ. sir ‘sun’ < OIA sūrī [13574]). However, semantically the Klm. verb matches with S. sūsṭu i.a. ‘a flock of birds’ (besides ‘a whizz, any rushing noise of wind’) and the Lithuanian reflex of PIE *ḱȗes(hx)- ‘breathe’ which is šušinu, šušinti ‘mit zischendem Geräusch durch die Luft fahren (wie der Blitz); to hurtle through the air with a whooshing noise (like a flash)’. Pokorny considers the Lith. form to be possibly a separate onomatopeic lemma together with Old High German sūsōn (and New High German sausen ‘to speed, fly, swish’, etc.) (IEW: 631). Köbler reconstructs with question-mark PIE *sūs- ? ‘sausen, einen brausenden oder zischenden Ton hervorbringen; to speed, fly; to produce a roaring or hissing sound’. In all likelihood, the Kalami verbal expression and the Sindhī noun belong to the Outer Languages. (b) Bng. śupīṇ n.f. ‘cobra’; Jaun. śūpāṇoi ‘serpent (ophiophagus and cobra class)’, śupiāṇ ‘cobra’ (Z.) < OIA *śuṣ(i)-sarpiṇī ‘hissing snake’ and not, as suggested by Turner, < OIA sarpiṇī ‘female snake’ (13274) (cf. Jaun. śuśkyārūṇȭ ‘to whistle’, Garh. suskārā ‘deep and loud breath’, Bshk. “shoshotîná” ‘to pant’, Jaṭ. ṭhaṭhā śukārā bharaṇ ‘to heave a sigh’ (more literal: ‘to fill a cold sigh’) and similar Khaś. śūk ‘hissing of a snake’, S. sūsṭu i.a. ‘a whizz, any rushing noise of wind’ (besides ‘a flock of birds’), M.hal. sīsᵃkāṛī ‘whistle’ (Grierson 1920) — borrowed into Brah. šūkār ‘whistling, whistle’, West Himalayish Kann. “shŭĩ̄ lonmig' ‘to whistle’, Munda Kh. siskari ‘to whistle’ (which is a borrowing from Sad. siskārī ‘whistling’) and Mu. susuān ‘to make a hissing sound’); Deog. śɔṅgau and śɔṅgaɔ, and Jaun. śãgyārō and śəṅṛiāṭ (Z.) all ‘snake’ < OIA *śuṣ(i)-nāga- ‘hissing snake’ plus some suffix, cf. also Jaun. śoṅgśiavṇɔ ‘to pant’ (Z.) with same derivation (*‘to hiss [like a] cobra’); cf. also Bng. śuśmɔ̃ n.m. ‘buzzing in one’s ears, buzzing sound of burning wet wood’ (with -mɔ̃ suffix) and śuśmāṇɔ ‘to blow loudly (e.g., into one’s hands), pant during possession’ — Kal. šišpẹ̃́ kárik ‘to whistle; to hiss (as a snake)’ is a synonym compound < OIA śuṣ(i)-švana- (see OIA svaná- ‘noise’ [13901]), Pr. viṣ ti- ‘to hiss (snake)’ — cf. also Shgh. sāɣ̌(d) ‘a big snake (in folklore), dragon’ and Bar. sāwn ‘a kind of dragon’ which is < *suṣ̌nā- with OIA (RV) parallel śúṣṇa- ‘’hisser’, name of a demon slain by Indra’, both of which ultimately derive < IIr. ćušnă̄- ‘snake, dragon’ (on this complex see also Morgenstierne [1975: 433] with some additional data). Note also OIA (RV v,33,5) ahiśuṣmastvan- ‘one whose attendants (the Maruts) hiss like serpents’. Note also Ind. ší̄tʰ ‘hiss (of a snake)’ with further references and which is the same as Brj.-Aw. sitkār ‘drawing in of the breath (in ecstasy, or in pain)’ (< OIA śvasta- ‘breathed’?), and cf. below Bng. śuśu ‘throat’.
